opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, not that much. When I was applying for PhD programs, I wasn't really thinking in terms of school rankings. At that stage, what mattered most was the advisor and the research environment. For me that was Zhuowen Tu. I'd read his work, I liked how he thought about problems, and it felt like a place where I could work on things I actually cared about.

There's a common mindset, especially among Chinese students, where you look at the overall ranking and treat it as the deciding factor. I understand why. It's a simple signal, and families care about it. But a PhD is very different from undergrad. You spend five or six years working closely with one person and a small group. If that relationship works, if you get the freedom and guidance you need, that matters far more than whether the school is ranked fifth or twentieth.

UCSD was also a good place for computer vision and machine learning, even if it wasn't always named alongside the very top schools. And San Diego is a nice place to live. You're not under constant pressure, so you have space to think. I think that was actually good for me.

Looking back, I'd tell students the same thing. Rankings are a rough proxy at best. Find the advisor and the problems you're excited about, because that's what shapes you as a researcher.

r001.rationale: The response describes UCSD’s reputation at the time and discusses rankings generally, but does not say its computer science standing is substantially stronger now than when Xie chose to attend.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not that much. When I was applying for PhD programs, I think a lot of students, especially coming from China, look at those overall university rankings very carefully, and I understand why, because it's the only signal you have when you don't know the field well yet. But by the time I was making the decision, I had figured out that for a PhD, the ranking of the school matters a lot less than who you're going to work with.

For me the real factor was Zhuowen Tu. I had read his work, I liked the kind of problems he was thinking about, and when I talked to him it felt like someone I could actually learn from and argue with for five years. That's what a PhD is. You're not consuming the university, you're basically apprenticing with one person and a small group around them.

And UCSD was a good place for that. The computer vision and machine learning community there was smaller than at some of the bigger-name schools, but it was very tight, very collaborative. I also had a lot of freedom, which I think mattered more than I realized at the time. Nobody was telling me exactly what to work on. I could go explore, make mistakes, and figure out my own taste.

Looking back, I think the thing I'd tell students is that the name on the diploma fades pretty quickly. What stays with you is your advisor, your peers, and the habits you form. If I had optimized for the ranking, I probably would have ended up somewhere that looked better on paper but fit me worse.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the importance of rankings and UCSD’s community at the time, but does not say UCSD’s computer science standing is stronger now than when Xie chose it.
